video.title: How Shoulder Rotation Syncs Your Contact

classification.reason: The coach explains how internal shoulder rotation timing dictates each player's individual contact point using pro video analysis and provides principles to find one's own contact zone.

problem.title_as_question: How does shoulder rotation determine your optimal forehand contact point?
problem.definition: Players often try to copy an arbitrary contact point (such as hitting far out in front), which leads to mishits and poor racket face control if it does not match where their shoulder naturally begins internal rotation.

symptoms.description: Hitting the ball straight into the ground or burying it due to a severely closed racket angle.
The strike feels uncomfortable, painful, or unnatural during the forward swing.

causes.statement: The ball is not met at the exact transition where internal shoulder rotation just starts, causing the shoulder to have rolled over too much.
Allowing internal shoulder rotation to occur before contact disrupts and closes the string angle prematurely.
A player tries to force an arbitrary contact point out in front despite their shoulder naturally releasing closer to the body.

angles.summary: The humerus externally rotates during the early forward swing and contact must coincide exactly with the start of internal rotation.
There is no single objective contact point in space; contact location depends on individual shoulder release timing.
Iga Swiatek releases her shoulder early and contacts the ball deeper with a bent elbow, while Roger Federer holds lag longer and contacts far in front.
The transition point can be felt naturally as the moment the shoulder stops stretching back and releases forward.

solutions.summary: Take a comfortable, painless pressing swing and identify the exact spatial spot where your shoulder humerus has just started to turn forward.
Use your feet and eyes to actively receive the ball directly into your shoulder's natural release spot, then fire and let the shoulder go.
solutions.external_goal: Actively receive the incoming ball into your specific transition zone.

solutions.summary: Progress by learning to feel your own shoulder release timing comfortably, matching your individual contact point to your swing rather than copying someone else's.
